item.title: 44 Ways to Know the Answer: The Insider Problem Inside Election Markets
item.description:
44 Ways to Know the Answer: The Insider Problem Inside Election Markets

The hardest contracts in this election are not who wins. They are the ones somebody already knows. Researchers call them knowable markets: contracts on candidate withdrawals, endorsements, debate appearances and rally remarks. The Anti-Corruption Data Collective counts an average of 44 of them tied to each individual race, and they have already traded more than $20 million.

The warning case is Maine. Researchers flagged dozens of suspicious, highly correlated trades on a Kalshi contract on whether Graham Platner would drop out of the Senate race, placed just before a damaging scandal became public. The trades do not prove insider trading, but they show the shape of the risk: the narrower the question, the fewer people hold the answer.

The exchanges are answering with enforcement. Kalshi told CNN it has suspended at least six 2026 candidates for betting on their own races, and its midterm transparency recap detailed four congressional cases: Mark Moran fined $6,229.30, Matt Klein $539.85 and Ezekiel Enriquez $784.20, each with five-year bans, and Laurie Buckhout just under $2,600 with a three-year suspension.

Washington is moving too. On October 5, Representative Don Davis introduced the No Betting on Your Own Race Act, with a penalty of $10,000 or three times the net gain, whichever is larger. Polymarket says it has hired a former FBI official to lead investigations and regularly refers cases to the Justice Department.

Two days out, that is the credibility trade. A market on who wins Congress aggregates thousands of strangers. A market on what one campaign does next can be settled by a handful of insiders, and everyone pricing it knows the difference.

Sources: CNN, Bonus, The Agent Bets, Anti-Corruption Data Collective

item.title: One Market Maker, Both Exchanges: Jump Trading Took a Piece of Each
item.description:
One Market Maker, Both Exchanges: Jump Trading Took a Piece of Each

Jump Trading, one of the biggest proprietary trading firms in the world, will reportedly gain stakes in both Kalshi and Polymarket in exchange for providing liquidity on the two exchanges. The terms differ by venue: a set amount of equity in Kalshi, while the Polymarket stake can expand over time if Jump meets certain capacity-providing objectives.

Liquidity is the unglamorous problem prediction markets have to solve. Market makers keep spreads tight and keep thin, less-heralded contracts functional until other traders arrive, and bringing in third-party firms also answers the concern that an operator's own internal desk is taking the other side of retail trades. Susquehanna, a Jump rival, has been making markets for prediction firms since 2024.

The prize is pricing. Sports contracts drive the industry's volume growth, yet through the 2025 NFL season pricing on Kalshi's NFL derivatives was consistently worse than what bettors found on DraftKings and FanDuel. Deeper professional liquidity is how the exchanges close that gap.

Small stakes here are not small money. The deals come days after Kalshi closed a $1 billion Series G at a $40 billion valuation, up from $22 billion in May, with Polymarket valued at $21 billion in its last round. As the reporting notes, even an unconfirmed half-percent stake in either company would be worth tens of millions of dollars. Kalshi already counts 500 institutional entities, a quarter of its volume outside market makers.

Jump is part of a pattern: CME Group partners on the DraftKings and FanDuel event-contract platforms, NYSE owner Intercontinental Exchange is Polymarket's largest investor, and Goldman Sachs calls the segment compelling. Wall Street's price-makers no longer just want to trade on these exchanges. They want to own a piece of them.

The Downside Is the Favorite: Bitcoin's November Ladder Leans to $72,500

November opened with Bitcoin's monthly ladder leaning down, not up. Polymarket's market asking what price Bitcoin will hit in November, which closes December 1 at 12:00 AM ET, prices a fall to $72,500 at 47 percent against a rise to $85,000 at 42 percent, on $171K traded in the last 24 hours. The downside leg is the favorite in the market's biggest monthly question.

Kalshi's separate question, how high Bitcoin gets in November, tells the same story in softer form. Traders there price Bitcoin above $82,500 at 57 percent, but above $87,500 at only 26 percent, in a market closing November 30 at 11:59 PM ET. A modest new high for the month is likely, on those prices. A breakout is not.

Ethereum mirrors the lean. Its November hit market, on $61K traded in 24 hours, prices a fall to $2,100 at 57 percent against a rise to $2,500 at 48 percent. On both of the two largest coins, the first big level traders expect to be touched this month is below the current price, not above it.

The near term is less bearish. Kalshi prices Bitcoin at $78,000 or above on November 6 at 5 PM ET at 51 percent, and $78,500 or above at 45 percent, on $76K traded in 24 hours. Its end-of-2026 range market puts the likeliest band at $75,000 to $79,999.99 at 18 percent, just ahead of $80,000 to $84,999.99 at 17 percent.

That caution is trading in size. DeFi Rate counts $164M of crypto contracts traded in 24 hours, and crypto is 12 percent of all prediction-market trading. For November, that money is not chasing a rally. It is pricing a dip first.

item.title: On NFL Sunday, Football Came Fourth: Esports and the NBA Took the Board
item.description:
On NFL Sunday, Football Came Fourth: Esports and the NBA Took the Board

It is an NFL Sunday, and on Polymarket the football is not where the money is. Of the ten highest-volume markets in the last 24 hours, not one is an NFL game. The board belongs to esports and basketball: Hanwha Life Esports against Bilibili Gaming drew $7.4 million in 24 hours, on $7.8 million traded in total, ahead of every American football contract on the platform.

The chasing pack tells the same story. Karmine Corp against Movistar KOI drew $4.5 million in 24 hours, Dota 2's Team Yandex against Team Spirit drew another $4.5 million, and the NBA's Cavaliers against Bucks drew $3.1 million, on $3.9 million in total. Three different sports, none of them the one filling stadiums this afternoon.

The contrast is sharpest across venues. On the cross-venue most-traded list, the busiest NFL game market, the Jets as 54 percent favourites, drew $2.4 million in 24 hours, and the Lions at 63 percent drew $2.0 million. A single League of Legends series on Polymarket traded roughly three times the busiest NFL game market.

This is the new shape of a sports Sunday. Polymarket counted 716 active markets and $195.5 million traded in 24 hours, $4.9 billion in total, and the flow follows start times around the world, not one league's calendar. Football still owns the afternoon in America. On the exchange, it now has to queue.
